title: Reinforcement Versus Punishment
objective: After this level you can tell positive and negative reinforcement and punishment apart in everyday examples.
summary: Positive adds and negative removes; reinforcement raises a behavior and punishment lowers it. The seatbelt beep is negative reinforcement, and time-out is negative punishment.

cards.headline: Your car's seatbelt beep is a lesson in negative reinforcement.
cards.body: The beeping stops the moment you buckle up. That isn't punishment, even though "negative" sounds like it should be. Two questions sort out all four terms for good.

cards.headline: Two questions to ask
cards.body: Skinner's terms use everyday words in a special way. First question: is something added or taken away? Positive means added, negative means removed; neither means good or bad. Second question: does the behavior go up or down? Reinforcement increases it, punishment decreases it. Both follow the law of effect from Level 25: satisfying consequences make a behavior more likely, unpleasant ones less likely.

items.label: Reinforcement: behavior goes up
points: Positive: add something good, like a toy for a clean room
Negative: remove something unpleasant, like the seatbelt beep

items.label: Punishment: behavior goes down
points: Positive: add something unpleasant, like a scolding for texting in class
Negative: remove something pleasant, like a favorite toy

cards.headline: The mix-up everyone makes
cards.body: Negative reinforcement is not punishment. Reinforcement, even the negative kind, always makes a behavior more likely; punishment always makes it less likely. The beep ends when you buckle, so you buckle more: that's reinforcement. Time-out is the one that trips people up. It removes a child from an enjoyable activity to make a behavior less likely, so it's negative punishment.

mascot.line: When in doubt, ask one thing: did the behavior go up? Then it's reinforcement, whatever the sign.

questions.explanation: Positive means something is added; negative means something is taken away.

questions.prompt: How does a seatbelt beep that stops when you buckle up change your behavior?

options.label: Removing the beep makes buckling likelier
Adding the beep makes buckling rarer
options.rationale: The beep pushes you to buckle, not to stop.

options.label: Removing a treat makes buckling rarer
options.rationale: No treat is involved, and buckling goes up.

options.label: Adding praise makes buckling likelier
options.rationale: Nothing pleasant is added; an annoyance is removed.

questions.explanation: It's negative reinforcement: an unpleasant sound is removed, so buckling up becomes more likely.

questions.prompt: Match each of Skinner's words with what it means.
